before: Either both are denied together or both are accepted together. Although one can reject both, one cannot choose only one. It is, however, easier for an unlawful union to be burdened with the fault of will while the fruitfulness of its seeds remains defended, than for the sexual act to be vindicated while its fruits are accused. Your wavering between fear and impiety will therefore not establish new rules of argument, allowing you to accept one of two connected things and exclude what belongs to it. “Light-footed deer will graze in the sky” (1 Corinthians 15:20–23) (Virgil, Eclogues 1.59) before a conclusion can be denied after its premise has settled the matter.

The apostle Paul uses this form of argument when he says, “If the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen. If Christ has not risen, your faith is empty” (1 Corinthians 15:16–17). But now Christ has risen; therefore it is certain that a day of resurrection awaits the dead (compare 1 Corinthians 15:20–23). To press this same point upon the reader with a shorter example: suppose there is doubt whether what is just is good. I ask whether you acknowledge that everything just is honorable. Once that is granted, I add another question: do you also pronounce everything honorable good? Once that too is granted, whether you like it or not, I conclude: if everything just is honorable, and everything honorable is good, then everything just is good. Anyone who tries to resist this conclusion after accepting the first premises does not shake reason’s structure but exposes himself to ridicule.

To bring the comparison back to the case: the question is whether sin exists in nature. I asked whether you would concede that no sin exists without will. You agreed, as your own words testify. I added whether you thought an infant possessed will. You denied this too. What follows as the third point, if sin does not exist without will? This is so certain that it cannot be doubted even by the Academics, whose wealth consists in holding nothing certain. So when you deny the third point after the first two premises, although it contains their conclusion, you do not overturn the foundations of reason: you reveal your frenzy.

before: He therefore says to Valerius: “Notice the arguments by which he thinks he agrees, against us, with the heading set out above. He says, ‘God, who had fashioned Adam from mud, built Eve from a rib and said: She will be called Life, because she is the mother of all the living’ (Genesis 3:20). That is not actually how it is written, but what does that matter to us? Memory commonly goes wrong over words, provided the meaning is retained. Nor was it God who named Eve Life, but her husband. The text says: ‘And Adam called his wife’s name Life, because she is the mother of all the living’” (Genesis 1:31) (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.4.12).

What astonishing learning in this teacher, who allows not even the slightest departure from Scripture’s language! He rebukes my ignorance, yet deigns to pardon the lapse of memory through which I had supposedly said that God called the woman by the name Life. He thus used a small opportunity to try to appear both learned and kind. But just as identifying who named the woman is no remarkable feat of diligence, so his shamelessness is intolerable when he wants to forgive something he cannot blame. For my work does not read as his inventions have it. I first quoted the Law’s testimony, where the Creator of all things is shown saying, “It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself” (Genesis 2:18). Then I said: “What does this mean, ‘It is not good for the human being to be alone’? Had God made anything that could rightly be called not good, especially when he had made everything not merely good but very good (compare Genesis 1:31)? How, then, does he say, ‘It is not good for the human being to be alone’? These words do not criticize the creature’s condition; they show that being alone could have been ruinous for the human race unless a succession of descendants had sprung up through the service of the other sex. For even if Adam may be thought capable of becoming immortal had he not sinned, it is nevertheless clear that he could never have become a father unless he had found a wife. Taken from his side while he slept, she heard at her first naming the work for which she had been prepared: ‘She will be called Life, because she is the mother of all the living.’ This statement showed that thereafter no human being could either exist or live without coming into existence through the benefit of conception” (compare Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.4.12).

It is therefore clear that, although the matter is not very weighty, I said nothing that anyone could criticize without extraordinary shamelessness. The stamp of public falsehood has been branded on this most destitute of men. By trying to give away what he does not possess, he offends in two ways at once: he lacks the right to do it, and he courts applause for his generosity.

before: “Yet even these,” he says, “you spared as human beings, and sent wasps ahead of the army—not because you lacked the power to subject the impious to the righteous in battle, but, judging little by little, you gave them room for repentance” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:8–10) (Genesis 9:20–27). “You pricked even those sacrilegious people,” he says in effect, “with the stings of flies, so that from the trivial instrument of their affliction they might recognize the avenger’s power.” After God’s purpose and the form of punishment made clear the voluntary sins whose rejection was awaited and sought, only then does the writer’s rebuke rise against the stubborn impiety of those punished. He says they had entered into such familiarity with crimes that these seemed in a way inborn. “You were not ignorant,” he says, “that their race had been most wicked, that their malice was natural, and that their thought could never be changed; for they were a cursed seed from the beginning. Nor did you grant pardon for their sins out of fear of anyone” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:10–11).

He means: “Although you so kindly and patiently granted time for repentance and set up a watchtower of warning, to defend your justice and mercy against every slander and every suspicion of cruelty, they nevertheless despised your warnings after despising your earlier benefits.” They acted as though wishing to prove that they came from the seed of Ham, against whom blessed Noah, after his nakedness was mocked, had hurled curses in fatherly judgment (compare Genesis 9:20–27). Why be surprised, then, that the writer recalled the severe sentence that had struck their ancestor for his insolence, to disgrace descendants who did not cease imitating him? In the Law, imitation by descendants is frequently rebuked using terms of kinship. Thus the Lord says to the Jews in the Gospel, “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44). Daniel is also read rebuking the filthy elders, though they came from Israel’s stock, in the same way: “Seed of Canaan, not of Judah” (Daniel 13:56; Susanna 56). The prophet Ezekiel likewise reproaches the people of Jerusalem: “Your mother was a Hittite and your father an Amorite” (Ezekiel 16:3, 45).

This is therefore an established usage: defamation of ancestry is added to blame of the will. A person appears to cling excessively to crime when, because of that crime, even his seed suffers insult. The same custom is also observed on the side of good people: when a man appears upright in every way, he is said to flourish with inborn virtues. Thus blessed Job affirms that he drew from the breasts the compassionate feeling with which he helped the needy, or rather that it came with him from his mother’s womb (Job 31:18). No comparison, exaggeration, or ambiguity can therefore count against plain facts. It is certain that mortals are never required to correct natural properties, yet God commands human beings to desist from evil. It is thus proved with the utmost truth that natural sin cannot exist.

before: Enough now about Genesis. Let us turn to the apostle Paul, whom Mani and the advocate of inherited sin think supports their opinion. Discussing the resurrection of the dead, he says: ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ’ (1 Corinthians 15:22) (Psalm 116:15). You, with whom we have our dispute, appropriated this testimony. But because you did not say what you thought it established, I can scarcely confirm it, though I suspect it.

What does it have to do with transmission of sin if everyone is said to die in Adam, when Adam is a human being’s name, while transmission denotes sin and Manichaean corruption? Unless perhaps you acknowledge Adam himself to be and to mean nothing other than sin, so that by this name the apostle seems to have pronounced that everyone dies in sin? But this is obviously insane.

What is strange, then, if, since the Hebrew word Adam means nothing other than ‘human’—as its translation expresses—the apostle said, ‘All die in Adam, and all will be made alive in Christ’: those who die according to human nature are raised from the dead through Christ’s power? Anyone denying this statement is mad. By the power of the same author who established fertility and mortality in this life, everyone will be raised from the graves, ‘so that each may receive what belongs to deeds done in the body, according to what was done, whether good or evil’ (2 Corinthians 5:10).

In the apostle’s saying, then, ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ,’ do you think he indicates bodily death, common to the just and unjust, or that penal death appointed for the devil and the ungodly? If this ordinary natural death, which in the saints is even precious (Psalm 116:15; LXX/Vulgate Psalm 115:6), and happens equally not only to good and evil people but also to humans and animals—if, I say, the apostle indicates this death—then plainly ‘Adam’ denotes human nature, while ‘Christ’ denotes the power of the Creator who raises the dead.

But if you want ‘All die in Adam’ to mean guilt rather than nature, an explanation is available as plain as it is certain: As all—that is, many—die by imitating Adam, so all—that is, many—are saved by imitating Christ. Either he spoke of common death and indicated nature, or of sin and condemned imitation. So he added shortly afterward: ‘As we have borne the image of the earthly one, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one’ (1 Corinthians 15:49). Certainly assuming the image could not be commanded if it were considered natural in either quality.

before: He persists in attacking us and adds: ‘As for those who have dared call this desire good against the evangelical and apostolic books, which they read to no purpose, you can see their saints sometimes sleeping with their daughters, sometimes carrying on with several concubines and wives. They do not see the apostle’s question: “What partnership is there between light and darkness, a believer and an unbeliever, Christ and Belial?” (2 Corinthians 6:14–15). They wander wrapped in desire’s cloud, enjoying its poison so much that, seized by madness, when they do this they think God has permitted it. As though they did not know the apostle said: “What they do in darkness is shameful even to mention” ’ (Ephesians 5:12).

You surely see how he presses the matter of shame and thinks it tells powerfully against us, because we dare not call evil what we nevertheless acknowledge must be covered through modesty. Thus you have woven no garment to cover your doctrine’s deformity except the rags you accepted in your father and teacher’s inheritance.

He keeps rising up against us and turns directly to his opponent: ‘Come, defender of desire, describe its fruits and works in plain words. See, in opposing it I do not fear the light which it dreads and hates. “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his deeds will not be exposed” (John 3:20). Do you see that desire is the source of evil, through which miserable souls serve lust unwillingly, because this is the only thing we do while the mind is unwilling?’

This is the source of your own statement: ‘Why is it that moving the lips, tongue, hands, and the bending of the back, neck, and sides for their proper tasks lies in our power, but when it comes to sowing children, the organs created for this task do not obey? Instead we wait for desire, as though acting under its own authority, to stir them; sometimes it fails to act when the mind is willing, although sometimes it acts when the mind is unwilling’ (Genesis 29:21–30) (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.7). You listed the functions of all the bodily members, emphasized their obedience to the will’s command, and said desire’s activity is the only thing we do against the mind’s will. What does Mani say? ‘Do you see that desire is the source of evil, through which miserable souls serve lust unwillingly, because this is the only thing we do while the mind is unwilling?’

But let us see what else he adds: ‘Every sin is outside the body, because it consists in action; but the fornicator sins against his own body (1 Corinthians 6:18). Every sin does not exist before it is committed, and afterward only the memory of the act remains, not its actual form. But desire’s evil, because it is natural, exists before it is enacted, increases while it is enacted, and afterward both appears and remains.’ Why, then, quarrel with us for calling you a Manichaean, when his writings contain nothing but what you say, and yours nothing but what he wants to persuade us to believe?

And that saying circulating on ordinary people’s lips, though put there by you, is contained in this same letter of Mani: If sin is not natural, why are infants baptized, when they plainly have done no evil themselves? I said it flies over many people’s tongues because it is a more popular argument, understood even by the slowest. In your books, however, you place your entire hope on it. Your teacher develops this very point as follows: ‘I must ask them in these words: If every evil consists in action, why does anyone receive purification by water before doing evil, when he has done no evil personally? Or if he has not yet acted but needs purification, it is possible to show that they are by nature shoots of evil stock—those very people whose madness prevents them from understanding either what they say or what they confidently affirm’ (compare 1 Timothy 1:7).

Do you hear how he insults us? He calls us mad and unable to understand what we say or affirm, because we deny that people are shoots of evil stock, although we baptize in purifying water even those who have done no evil—that is, infants. Many passages from his statements have now been quoted. Yet if the heading did not name his daughter Menoch and Mani, who calls himself Christ’s apostle, they would altogether announce you as their author (see this work 3.172). Since you say nothing except what you learned from Mani’s teaching, do you think catholics should regard you differently from the man through whom you drank in the mysteries of these doctrines?

He testifies why God wished the seven nations to perish, after whose destruction for the most part the promised land was given to the Israelites (compare Deuteronomy 7:1–2). According to you, he should certainly have added: because they were generated from a devilish union; because the ruler of darkness possessed them; because Adam infected everyone who would come from his stock. Only deeds committed through free will. “You hated them,” he says, “because they did deeds hateful to you.” (Deuteronomy 7:1–2)

But so that we would not be ignorant of the deeds, and so that you could not call these acts of the nations reproductive desire, he details the kinds of action themselves. “Through spells,” he says, “and unjust sacrifices; and they were merciless killers of children.” That is, they served sorcery and sacrifices that were unjust because they were offered to idols, after worship of the Creator had been abandoned. before: I certainly will not attack those who think Adam, had he obeyed, could have been transferred to immortality as a reward. We read that Enoch and Elijah were taken away so as not to see death (Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5; 2 Kings 2:11). But nature’s arrangements are one thing, rewards for obedience another. One person’s merit is not so great as to overturn everything established naturally. Inborn mortality would therefore have continued operating in the rest, even if that first human had passed from prolonged life to eternity.

This rests not on a conjecture open to denial but on a certain example: Enoch’s children could not be freed from the condition of dying by their father’s immortality. Nor should anyone perhaps object that, if not sinners, at least all the righteous would have reached immortality without intervening bodily dissolution. Abel, first among the righteous, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and every company of saints in both Testaments displayed their merit through virtues and their nature through death.

Christ’s authority also confirmed this settled matter. The Sadducees put a question to him using a woman married seven times, asking which husband would chiefly claim her if bodily resurrection were believed. He answered: ‘You are mistaken, knowing neither the Scriptures nor God’s power (Genesis 5:24). In the resurrection they neither marry nor take wives, for they will not die’ (Matthew 22:29–30; Luke 20:35–36). Knowing his own work, he explained why he had instituted marriage: reproduction would make up death’s losses. Generous fertility would cease at once when grasping death ceased.

If, then, Christ who created it testifies that fertility was made to contend with frailty, and marriage’s condition was arranged before sin, mortality too plainly belongs not to transgression but to nature, to which we read marriage also belongs. The law promulgated—‘On the day you eat what is forbidden, you shall surely die’ (Genesis 2:17) (Hebrews 11:5)—therefore means penal death, not bodily death. It threatens sins, not reproductive seed; only transgression incurs it, and only reform escapes it.

Its being said to fall on the day of sin follows Scripture’s practice of calling condemned someone still to be condemned. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Everyone who has not believed in me is already judged, because he has not believed in the name of God’s only-begotten (2 Kings 2:11) Son’ (John 3:18). This does not mean that unbelief denying Christ was already joined to eternal punishment before the time of judgment, since everyone who comes to faith was formerly an unbeliever. Rather, to display the lawgiver’s judgment, sins are spoken of as already punishments. Finally, both the book called Wisdom and many people’s opinion affirm that Adam himself was cleansed through subsequent reform (Wisdom of Solomon 10:1–2).

before: Enough about the woman; let us pass to the man’s tasks. ‘To Adam he said: The earth is cursed in your works. In sorrow you shall eat from it all the days of your life. It shall produce thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the grass of your field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken, because you are earth, and into earth you shall go’ (Genesis 3:17–19) (Genesis 4:7). Here he did not say, ‘I will multiply your thorns or your sweat’ (Genesis 1:11–12); they are spoken of as though first created then. Yet this objection is removed with no greater effort than in his wife’s case.

First, it is not the human’s seed but the soil that is cursed: ‘The earth will be cursed in your works.’ What had the fields done to deserve the insult of a curse for the sin of someone else’s will, when they certainly could inherit nothing from Adam? Was it to teach by the very sods that a curse can exist where no fault exists? If sin was in the human but the curse in the crop, plainly guilt does not always attach to loss.

If the earth is cursed to afflict the sinner, while iniquity is not located where the curse is, why could the same condition not apply even if some miseries were shown to have been imposed on our nature after the first human’s sin? It would not follow that newborns are miserable to prove them guilty. Rather, by recalling the first sin, suffering handed down could warn against evil imitation those whom it had not made guilty. The earth likewise would be shown to have endured the insult of a curse to condemn the evil of another’s will, not to generate participation in its own guilt. Unless perhaps we believe soil dearer to God than innocence, so that while he does not allow another’s crime to pollute a clod, he nevertheless permits it to condemn infancy!

The curse is directed at the earth, then, but even this is not left unexplained. The purpose of the pronouncement and the way the soil is called cursed are set out: ‘In sorrow you shall eat from it all the days of your life.’ Notice how he explains himself. The earth is called cursed not because punishment could be inflicted on it, but because this name expresses the opinion of a grieving mind. Knowing it barren because of its cultivator’s deserts, the hungry worker in his distress would blame the soil for what he had himself deserved. Afflicted, he would call it cursed. Its fertility was withheld precisely so that the transgressor should acknowledge neither nature nor earth, but his own will and person, as subject to the curse.

before: First, how insane is your very claim that childbirth pain accompanies sin! It so plainly concerns the condition of the sexes rather than punishment for crimes that all animals, stained by no sin, undergo these pangs and groans in giving birth. This shows that something found even without sin is not proof of sin.

Then you advance another, far more foolish claim. ‘A woman would not suffer pain,’ you say, ‘unless she shared in crimes.’ Yet immediately you add: ‘But this sin, for which the woman suffers, is found not in the mother but in the child being born.’ (1 Corinthians 11:3) Thus, you say, even baptized women live free from sin, yet are afflicted by the difficulties of their childbearing because of the iniquity of the children they bring forth. On this opinion, inherited sin no longer flows from mother to offspring but pours back from the newborn into the parents. If a baptized woman feels pain because iniquities are found in the infant, transmission begins to run uphill rather than downhill.

‘But she is not tormented because her son has iniquity; rather, because she herself brought it with her when she was born.’ Yet you said grace removed this evil from her. If a laboring woman’s pain adhered to sin, removing sin should have cured childbirth’s torment. Or, if this torment cannot exist without iniquity, but is still found in women after baptism, then grace has not removed their iniquity either, and baptism’s ceremony has become worthless.

But if these mysteries possessed the power and truth we believe in, not what you invent, and every sin was removed, yet the pain caused by difficult childbirth remains, it is clear that this groaning indicates nature, not fault. Even you agree it is suffered by women whom you acknowledge freed from the Manichaeans’ sin. So much is clear from examples alone. If we inspect the words of the pronouncement itself, however, it will dissolve your fog with brilliance surpassing the sun’s rays.

The woman was not told, ‘Pains will arise within you,’ or, ‘I will create groaning for you,’ as though these sensations were instituted after her fault. Rather: ‘I will greatly multiply your sorrows’ (Genesis 3:16). God shows that what he promises not to create but to multiply in the sinful person already exists in the natural order. Only existing things are multiplied. Before they exist, ‘making’ is the proper expression; calling it ‘increasing’ is premature.

Lest this seem our own point rather than truth’s, this same order of words is recorded concerning all living beings. Before humanity was made, God said: ‘Let us make humanity in our image and likeness’ (Genesis 1:26). Again concerning the woman: ‘God said: It is not good for the human to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself’ (Genesis 2:18). After they were made, however: ‘He blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply and fill the earth’ (Genesis 1:28). Before their creation he did not say ‘Let them multiply,’ but ‘Let humanity be made.’ Once someone existed who could increase, he appropriately added, ‘Increase and multiply and fill the earth.’

In this same order, childbirth’s groaning, established naturally in human bodies as in animals, was not created in Eve but increased, so that she would suffer a special intensity of heightened pangs. Yet these would reach later women only in the ordinary natural measure, varying with their bodies. Thus sin did not cause the woman to suffer in childbirth, but to suffer excessively. Similarly, we read of bodily infirmities coming upon particular people for sins at different times; but such increased misery did not overturn the smaller natural measure.

Not everything in this pronouncement, however, is confined to punitive severity. One part indicates desert, another specifies a duty. ‘I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning; in sorrow you shall bear children.’ Up to this point comes punishment, earned by the person, not by nature. From here the task of the sex created second is simply described: ‘Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you’ (Genesis 3:16). This plainly does not concern punishment: its absence would concern fault. A woman’s submission to her husband with modest affection belongs to order, not punishment. According to the apostle, ‘the husband is the woman’s head’ (Ephesians 5:23), because ‘man was not created for woman, but woman for man’ (1 Corinthians 11:9). If she reveres her head with fitting modesty, she maintains nature’s arrangements rather than enduring sin’s torments. If she resists that order, she is guilty. Performing something whose neglect is a fault is therefore no misery.

before: But let us examine the rest. I think the reader has been instructed more than enough by what we have treated about the strength with which he either attacks anything in my statements or defends his own opinion. It will therefore not be necessary to demonstrate this by repeating all his writings. For he puts before himself scarcely more than isolated, scattered little lines from my book, often praising them and sometimes tickling them with the briefest criticism. Yet what he thinks he should bite at was not said by me in the way he supposes. I therefore direct the reader to my work: he will see that its argument agrees with truth.

This man, who complained that I accused him of attacking nature and seeds, could not endure continuous pretense. After soothing his patron’s hearing with tricks, he puts out his head like a tortoise. He had said that, unless Adam had sinned, people could have generated children as we ordinarily move our joints or trim our nails. Then he added: “But if the seed itself carries no curse, what does this passage in the book of Wisdom mean? ‘You were not ignorant that their race was wicked, that their malice was natural, and that their thought could never be changed; for they were a cursed seed from the beginning’” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:10–11) (Psalm 58:4–5). He follows the testimony with this argument: “Surely, whoever these words concern, they concern human beings” (compare Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.6.17–2.9.21).

Here is the man who professed to have abandoned Manichaean pursuits! Taking an opportunity from a statement he does not understand, he pronounces the seed cursed, malice natural, and the thought of the unjust incapable of change. It is said that those living beside the Nile’s cataracts have lost their hearing from the roar of the falling waters. Perhaps rumor invented that, spreading larger tales from great things. Still, the example serves to rebuke the deafness of fools who resist the voice of facts like deaf adders, amid the din of mutual intimidation (compare Psalm 58:4–5; LXX Psalm 57:5–6). Augustine cries: “The human race is wicked; its malice is natural; its thought forever unchangeable; its seed cursed from the beginning.” And there are still people who think he has not been stamped all over with Manichaeus’s mark! Let the public followers of that filth be questioned today. If they say anything different, let us be judged liars.

So if malice is natural, how do you pretend not to pronounce nature evil? If the seed is cursed from the beginning, how do you say you accuse the vices of wills, not of seeds? If evildoers’ thought cannot be changed, how do you falsely swear that you acknowledge free choice? Unless the only thing left is for you to say that those Hebrews, Sirach or Philo, who are uncertainly believed to have authored the book called Wisdom, were Manichaeans.

I think the reader has been instructed more than enough by what we have treated about the strength with which he either attacks anything in my statements or defends his own opinion. It will therefore not be necessary to demonstrate this by repeating all his writings. For he puts before himself scarcely more than isolated, scattered little lines from my book, often praising them and sometimes tickling them with the briefest criticism. Yet what he thinks he should bite at was not said by me in the way he supposes. I therefore direct the reader to my work: he will see that its argument agrees with truth.

This man, who complained that I accused him of attacking nature and seeds, could not endure continuous pretense. After soothing his patron’s hearing with tricks, he puts out his head like a tortoise. He had said that, unless Adam had sinned, people could have generated children as we ordinarily move our joints or trim our nails. Then he added: “But if the seed itself carries no curse, what does this passage in the book of Wisdom mean? ‘You were not ignorant that their race was wicked, that their malice was natural, and that their thought could never be changed; for they were a cursed seed from the beginning’” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:10–11) (Wisdom 12:10-11). He follows the testimony with this argument: “Surely, whoever these words concern, they concern human beings” (compare Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.6.17–2.9.21).

Here is the man who professed to have abandoned Manichaean pursuits! Taking an opportunity from a statement he does not understand, he pronounces the seed cursed, malice natural, and the thought of the unjust incapable of change. It is said that those living beside the Nile’s cataracts have lost their hearing from the roar of the falling waters. Perhaps rumor invented that, spreading larger tales from great things. Still, the example serves to rebuke the deafness of fools who resist the voice of facts like deaf adders, amid the din of mutual intimidation (compare Psalm 58:4–5; LXX Psalm 57:5–6). Augustine cries: “The human race is wicked; its malice is natural; its thought forever unchangeable; its seed cursed from the beginning.” And there are still people who think he has not been stamped all over with Manichaeus’s mark! Let the public followers of that filth be questioned today. If they say anything different, let us be judged liars.

So if malice is natural, how do you pretend not to pronounce nature evil? If the seed is cursed from the beginning, how do you say you accuse the vices of wills, not of seeds? If evildoers’ thought cannot be changed, how do you falsely swear that you acknowledge free choice? Unless the only thing left is for you to say that those Hebrews, Sirach or Philo, who are uncertainly believed to have authored the book called Wisdom, were Manichaeans.

before: “Yet even these,” he says, “you spared as human beings, and sent wasps ahead of the army—not because you lacked the power to subject the impious to the righteous in battle, but, judging little by little, you gave them room for repentance” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:8–10) (Wisdom 12:8). “You pricked even those sacrilegious people,” he says in effect, “with the stings of flies, so that from the trivial instrument of their affliction they might recognize the avenger’s power.” After God’s purpose and the form of punishment made clear the voluntary sins whose rejection was awaited and sought, only then does the writer’s rebuke rise against the stubborn impiety of those punished. He says they had entered into such familiarity with crimes that these seemed in a way inborn. “You were not ignorant,” he says, “that their race had been most wicked, that their malice was natural, and that their thought could never be changed; for they were a cursed seed from the beginning. Nor did you grant pardon for their sins out of fear of anyone” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:10–11).

He means: “Although you so kindly and patiently granted time for repentance and set up a watchtower of warning, to defend your justice and mercy against every slander and every suspicion of cruelty, they nevertheless despised your warnings after despising your earlier benefits.” They acted as though wishing to prove that they came from the seed of Ham, against whom blessed Noah, after his nakedness was mocked, had hurled curses in fatherly judgment (compare Genesis 9:20–27). Why be surprised, then, that the writer recalled the severe sentence that had struck their ancestor for his insolence, to disgrace descendants who did not cease imitating him? In the Law, imitation by descendants is frequently rebuked using terms of kinship. Thus the Lord says to the Jews in the Gospel, “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44). Daniel is also read rebuking the filthy elders, though they came from Israel’s stock, in the same way: “Seed of Canaan, not of Judah” (Daniel 13:56; Susanna 56). The prophet Ezekiel likewise reproaches the people of Jerusalem: “Your mother was a Hittite and your father an Amorite” (Ezekiel 16:3, 45).

This is therefore an established usage: defamation of ancestry is added to blame of the will. A person appears to cling excessively to crime when, because of that crime, even his seed suffers insult. The same custom is also observed on the side of good people: when a man appears upright in every way, he is said to flourish with inborn virtues. Thus blessed Job affirms that he drew from the breasts the compassionate feeling with which he helped the needy, or rather that it came with him from his mother’s womb (Job 31:18). No comparison, exaggeration, or ambiguity can therefore count against plain facts. It is certain that mortals are never required to correct natural properties, yet God commands human beings to desist from evil. It is thus proved with the utmost truth that natural sin cannot exist.

before: Having explained God’s patience and his most gentle ordering of things, by which he does not desire the death of the dying person but rather that he turn back and live (compare Ezekiel 18:32; 33:11), the writer continues to prove what he said by examples. He mentions those whose terribly wicked lives in the land of Canaan had kindled the Almighty’s anger, so that the land would be granted, through the most just punishment, to the victories of the Israelites, now living under God’s law. “Hating those ancient inhabitants of your holy land, because they did hateful deeds before you through spells and unjust sacrifices, and were merciless killers of children, you willed to destroy them through our fathers’ hands, so that the land dearest to you of all lands might receive a worthy settlement of God’s children” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:3–7) (Ezekiel 18:32).

He testifies why God wished the seven nations to perish, after whose destruction for the most part the promised land was given to the Israelites (compare Deuteronomy 7:1–2). Lest God appear to distinguish persons by partiality within one human nature, he explains why the Canaanites deserved to be killed. “You hated,” he says, “those ancient inhabitants of your holy land.” (Wisdom 12:3) Why? According to you, he should certainly have added: because they were generated from a devilish union; because the ruler of darkness possessed them; because Adam infected everyone who would come from his stock. But he says none of these things. What reason does he give for the hatred? Only deeds committed through free will. “You hated them,” he says, “because they did deeds hateful to you.” (Deuteronomy 7:1–2)

But so that we would not be ignorant of the deeds, and so that you could not call these acts of the nations reproductive desire, he details the kinds of action themselves. “Through spells,” he says, “and unjust sacrifices; and they were merciless killers of children.” That is, they served sorcery and sacrifices that were unjust because they were offered to idols, after worship of the Creator had been abandoned. To these sacrileges they devoted their own relatives, appeasing demons even by the enormity of murdering their children. See, then, how far he is from speaking of the crime Manichaeus invents, a crime naturally adhering to every mortal. He recalls that their chief offense was that they did not refrain even from destroying their own little children. Those children’s deaths would not bring odium on the killer if both the murderer and the child displeased God because of one and the same sin.
